title: Understanding factors that influence time to surgery for hip fractures in South Africa: A qualitative study using the Model of Pathways to Treatment
content:
by Sarah Drew, Bilkish Cassim, Rudo M. S. Chingono, Farhanah Paruk, Mkhululi Lukhele, Cliff Zinyemba, Anu Abraham, Kimberly Lakin, Matt L. Costa, Celia L. Gregson, Rachael Gooberman-Hill

Although early surgery for hip fractures (HF) improves patient outcomes, in South Africa (SA) time to surgery often exceeds recommended durations. We explore factors influencing time to HF surgery in SA to inform interventions promoting earlier access. Data were collected through repeated in-depth interviews with 38 HF patients and their caregivers and 40 healthcare professionals (HCPs) and observations of clinical practice in five hospitals in Gauteng. Findings were informed by the four key “intervals” of the ‘Model of Pathways to Treatment’. Appraisal: Personal beliefs that symptoms were due to other causes or that hospital visits were a “weakness”, prompted initial self-management. Early care-seeking was prompted by pain intensity and further encouraged by family members. Help-seeking: Timely access to transport was impacted by ambulance shortages, long distances, and safety concerns for paramedics, and thus many patients relied on private transportation. High-impact trauma cases were prioritised over low-impact HF. Diagnostic: Patient pathways varied and were complicated by ambulance shortages and scheduling issues. Administrative requirements (referral letters) slowed referral processes, particularly for patients from outside hospital catchment areas. Caregivers found admission paperwork burdensome, while HCPs viewed it as helpful for coordinating care and avoiding later delays. While hospitals prioritised emergency cases (including HF), HCPs felt streamlining administrative processes could improve time to X-ray. Pre-treatment: Patients and caregivers reported long waits for surgery, with delays leading to complications and further setbacks. Surgeries were often postponed for other “emergencies”, with HCPs describing difficulties with managing competing surgical priorities. This study, the first to explore factors that impact time to HF surgery in SA, highlights the agency of patients and caregivers in negotiating access to treatment, and health system processes that help or hinder access. Findings identify key leverage points for interventions targeted at each ‘interval’ in the care pathway to accelerate access to HF surgery.
